title: Where are the most jobs for 18-24 year-olds?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByTommy LumbyBusiness data journalist and Nick EdserBusiness reporterUpdated 3 minutes agoIf you're one of the nearly one mi
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByTommy LumbyBusiness data journalist and Nick EdserBusiness reporterUpdated 3 minutes agoIf you're one of the nearly one million people aged 16-24 not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet" - then you might be wondering where to start.Under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work, a major review aimed at cutting the number of Neets will say.But how many jobs are there where you live? Use our look-up tool to find out.Where are the available jobs?Where you live will often have a big impact on your ability to find a job.We have used online job adverts to help identify the number of vacancies suitable for young people in the area they live, relative to the size of the local population.The Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) think tank used AI to help identify the jobs, which were broadly defined as roles requiring relatively low experience or education.According to its analysis, South Oxfordshire had 387 suitable vacancies per 1,000 18 to 24-year-olds in the area - the most of any local authority. Rotherham had the least, at 53 per 1,000.Use this tool to check out the situation in your area. The data for London is only available for the region as a whole and is not broken down by individual councils.Which sectors have the most entry-level jobs?Even if there are jobs available in your area, you might not find one in the sector you want to work in.The sector with the highest average number of entry-level vacancies in the year to October was teaching, with most of those jobs being for teaching assistants, learning support and cover supervisor roles, according to jobs website Adzuna.The next largest was hospitality and catering, traditionally an area where younger people get their first experience of work.Adzuna, a major online jobs website, includes adverts for full-time roles marked as entry-level, those asking for up to two years' experience, graduate roles, internships and apprenticeships.Accounting and finance had the third-highest number of job openings.What are the typical rates of pay?Figures on salaries for vacancies can be patchy because many employers do not include them in job adverts.Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently urged businesses to start publishing salaries ahead of plans to make pay details compulsory in adverts.Only about 40% of Adzuna's jobs data for the year to October stated a salary, although that figure varies widely by sector.Here are the average salaries for jobs in the sectors with the largest number of entry-level jobs, according to Adzuna. The highest average salary is £30,530 in engineering, while social care has the lowest at £25,880.How many job vacancies are there overall?While it can be hard for anyone looking for their first job, the situation is also tough for older jobseekers.Across the whole economy there were 690,000 jobs available in the August to October period this year, which is the lowest number since early 2021.The Covid pandemic led to huge swings in the number of job vacancies available as companies reacted to shutdowns and then reopened as restrictions were lifted.Stripping out the fluctuations seen during the pandemic, the number of vacancies is now at its lowest level for 12 years.Apprenticeships have often been a way for people to get their first taste of employment.In England the number of people starting apprenticeships has risen in recent years, although this has been driven by an increase in those aged 25 and over after schemes for older workers were fully rolled out in 2008.The number of people aged 24 and under starting apprenticeships in England in 2025 was 172,230, down from a peak of 291,300 in 2012.

schema.headline: Where are the most jobs for 18-24 year-olds?

title: Government must act now or lose Royal Mail, former minister Peter Kyle warns
description: Former Business Secretary Peter Kyle has said the government must act urgently to "level the playing field" for Royal Mail or risk the business becomi
body: Former Business Secretary Peter Kyle has said the government must act urgently to "level the playing field" for Royal Mail or risk the business becoming unviable.He said he was concerned that the firm was being "undercut" by rival parcel delivery firms who did not employ staff under the same conditions.Royal Mail, which is owned by International Distribution Services, has struggled in recent years with increased competition, fewer letters being sent and fines from the regulator for missing delivery targets.A government spokesperson said it would consider whether further reforms are required to the parcel market after the watchdog, Ofcom, publishes its annual monitoring report  in December.Kyle had started to prepare officials at the Department for Business and Trade (DBT) to look at the delivery market for parcels shortly before he was replaced in his job by Jonathan Reynolds as business secretary in July.He said a "crunch point" had been reached where the government had to make a decision about whether it wants Royal Mail "to be a viable proposition in the future".He said his review would have looked at where the costs in that market lay and where the profit was being made, to see successful companies upheld "the values of business in Britain today"."If we leave it another few years then Royal Mail will just become unviable and it will just collapse under the weight of having full-time employees," he said.According to Royal Mail, 98% of its 130,000 workers are permanent employees, with rights to benefits including pensions, sick pay and holiday pay.Some other parcel delivery companies use self-employed delivery drivers, with some offering an opt-in service that gives couriers limited additional benefits.Royal Mail is also legally obliged to offer customers a "one price goes anywhere" service across the UK and to deliver first class letters six days a week to every address.Kyle's proposed review would not have considered further changes to Royal Mail's universal service obligations or to terms and conditions for its staff.

schema.headline: Government must act now or lose Royal Mail, former minister Peter Kyle warns

title: Bilkis Bano: Gujarat riots gang-rape survivor 'heartbroken' after Supreme Court bail for two convicts
description: The article has details that some readers may find disturbingA pregnant Muslim woman who was gang-raped and saw 14 family members murdered during the
body: The article has details that some readers may find disturbingA pregnant Muslim woman who was gang-raped and saw 14 family members murdered during the 2002 Gujarat riots has spoken of her "pain, shock and disbelief" after two of her rapists were recently granted bail.Bilkis Bano said in a statement that she heard about the top court order through press reports and vowed to fight back. The freed men are from a group of 11 convicts - part of a Hindu mob - serving life terms for the attack on Bano.All the men were also freed in 2022 after a Gujarat government order. That decision, and the celebrations as they left prison, caused global outrage. In 2024, the Supreme Court overturned the order.In a short three-page order dated 28 October, the Supreme Court granted bail to Bipinchand Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya and suspended their sentences while their petition challenging a 2017 Bombay High Court order is being heard.The judges explained that the early release was because the two convicts "have been under incarceration for a period of more than 17 years" and "that one of the appellants has a severe handicap". On Tuesday, Bano's lawyer Shobha Gupta told the BBC that the news of Joshi and Modhiya's release had left "Bilkis heartbroken"."She has to restart her battle for justice. She had no information that this case was coming up in the Supreme Court. What is troubling for us is that every time something like this happens, we worry that it could affect her faith in judiciary." Gupta said it was difficult to understand why the convicts were being released because "it's not a routine criminal case, it's a case that shocks the conscience of the world, of entire humanity".The attack on Bano and her family was one of the most horrific crimes during the Gujarat riots, which began after 60 Hindu pilgrims were killed in a fire on a passenger train in the town of Godhra.Hindu mobs attacked Muslim neighbourhoods, blaming them for starting the fire. The riots continued for three days and more than 1,000 people died, most of them Muslims.When rioters attacked Bano's village and started setting Muslim homes on fire, she and 16 relatives went on the run. She was 19, had a three-year-old daughter and was pregnant with her second child. They were attacked on the morning of 3 March 2002 by a group of men "with swords and sticks", she'd told me in 2017. Her three-year-old daughter, she said, was snatched from her lap and killed.How a Gujarat riot victim stood up to her rapistsIndia Supreme Court cancels release of 2002 riots rapistsIndia PM Modi's government okayed rapists' releaseHer attackers were her neighbours, men she had seen almost daily while growing up. They tore off her clothes and several of them raped her, ignoring her pleas for mercy.Her cousin, who had given birth two days earlier, was raped and murdered and her newborn baby was killed too.Bano survived only because she lost consciousness and her attackers left, believing she was dead. Two boys - seven and four - were the only other survivors of the massacre.Her fight for justice has been long and nightmarish. The first arrests were made only in 2004 after the Supreme Court called in federal investigators and transferred her case to Mumbai, saying that courts in Gujarat could not deliver justice to her.In her statement released on Monday night, Bano spoke of "fresh tears of pain, shock and disbelief"."I still cannot believe that once again, for the second time, an order has been passed by the Supreme Court without calling me up and without hearing me," she said."For 24 long years, I have stood up to fight for justice... again and again. Yet today, I find myself losing the very justice I had fought so hard to win.... And I am scared of losing faith in justice, yet again." Bano vowed to "fight this order... for my children, who do not deserve to live haunted by fears and scars for the rest of their lives". "I do this for my three-year-old Saleha who deserved to live and whose memory demands justice. I do this for women everywhere. Because no woman, no survivor, no citizen should have to endure this eternal test of belonging and equality, and fight for justice for the rest of her life."Prime Minister Narendra Modi was Gujarat chief minister at the time of the riots, and was criticised for not doing enough to prevent the carnage. He has always denied wrongdoing and has not apologised for the riots.In 2013, a Supreme Court panel also said that there was insufficient evidence to prosecute him. But critics have continued to blame him for the riots happening on his watch.

schema.headline: Bilkis Bano: Gujarat riots gang-rape survivor 'heartbroken' after Supreme Court bail for two convicts

title: Putin's Crimea bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
description: Figure caption, Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimea bridgeByOlivia IrelandSarah RainsfordSouthern and Eastern Europe correspondent, Kyiv a
body: Figure caption, Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimea bridgeByOlivia IrelandSarah RainsfordSouthern and Eastern Europe correspondent, Kyiv and Ilya AbishevBBC News RussianUpdated 1 hour agoUkraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge - also known as the Kerch Bridge - has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Russia's war effort.A Kremlin spokesperson insisted the bridge would be rebuilt "better than before".Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Northern and Southern bridges, both important crossings over the Dnipro River, were closed after Russia targeted the Ukrainian capital overnight.Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.The damage reported on Tuesday appeared to be far more severe than previously, with a large arched section of the bridge apparently destroyed.Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.Zelensky said the overnight strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".He said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and a Russian-backed official said some rail services were operating. The bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014, and was personally opened by Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2018.While Ukraine has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Putin.The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry. Image source, EPAImage caption, There was heavy traffic in Kyiv on Tuesday after two major crossings were closed after strikes Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water.Some of Kyiv's above-ground subway services were damaged in the overnight attacks, officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.Strikes on the busy Northern and Southern Bridges will cause major disruption to people's daily lives.Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the Cherkasy region, according to local officials.The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.The collapse of the arched section of the Crimean Bridge has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired.However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Ukraine has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar. This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel. This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdiansk.Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

schema.headline: Putin's Crimea bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine

title: Komyshuvakha: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after strikes that killed 57
description: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72Image source, Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing via
body: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72Image source, Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty ImagesByMerlyn Thomas BBC Verify correspondent and Paul BrownBBC VerifyUkrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people.Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it said was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.Verified images posted in the days after the attack show damage to emergency vehicles and excavation equipment at the site. The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) told BBC Verify there were multiple Russian strikes during the rescue. The DSNS said three police officers, four workers and two rescue dogs were injured while five vehicles were damaged during the operation, which has now concluded.With the DSNS saying the death toll had risen to at least 72 people, the attack on Komyshuvakha has become the second deadliest single incident of the Ukraine war.Image source, DSNSImage caption, Emergency service vehicles have also been targetedOleksiy, an intelligence officer investigating the incident for Ukraine's SBU security service, who asked to be identified only by his first name, said rescue vehicles were "clearly marked" and accused Russia of "deliberately destroying humanitarian equipment".He added the village's infrastructure and the people still living in Komyshuvakha are also being systematically targeted by drones and bombs. Oleksiy accused Russian forces of "outright terror against civilians, against peaceful residents" to make life on the front line impossible.BBC Verify has confirmed videos being shared by Ukrainian police that show rescue workers at the scene shouting "drone, drone" and running for cover on the day after the 2 November attack. A group can also be seen treating a victim.Image source, DSNSOleksiy said rescue crews operated under a constant threat of attack. "The enemy knows perfectly well that what is being carried out there is essentially a humanitarian operation to search for the dead," he said.BBC Verify has asked the Russian Ministry of Defence for comment specifically about the Komyshuvakha attacks but has not received a response.A general statement released on 2 November by the Russian MoD said it had targeted energy and transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian military across the country.While there are no military or industrial facilities in Komyshuvakha it is close to a key route used for Ukrainian troop movements, supplies and evacuations. The village was previously reported to have been struck by the Russians on 28 October.Fears of second strike heard on police radiosLocal people headed to the shelter area on 2 November after being told by a local Telegram group that aid would be distributed between 10:00 and 12:00 local time (08:00-10:00 GMT). Ukrainian authorities said an initial strike, at 09:45 local time, hit buildings above ground killing one woman.Figure caption, Video shows moments between deadly Russian attacks on village in UkraineBodycam footage, released by Ukrainian police in edited segments and analysed by BBC Verify, shows people trying to free a casualty from the rubble before declaring she had died.Throughout the footage, warnings of an impending second strike can be heard on police radios with increasing urgency until people are instructed to run to the underground shelter.The same footage, which was taken around an hour after the first attack, goes on to show people in a shelter. As they wait in silence a large explosion can be heard and the video goes dark.Aftermath video filmed later shows bodies being recovered from a large crater immediately above the shelter. Twisted iron and rubble from the structure below can be seen beneath the surface.Funerals have been held almost daily for the victims of the attack, including locals working to administer aid distribution, those seeking to collect it and soldiers who officials say arrived to assist with rescue efforts.Image source, Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty ImagesTrevor Ball, bomb disposal expert at intelligence firm at Armament Research Services, said a crater seen in the footage was consistent with the damage and depth left by a FAB-3000, a 3,000kg Russian bomb which can destroy underground structures. His comments were echoed by Chris Proops, an ex-UK National Crime Agency investigator, who said the scale of the damage at the scene matched the size of the FAB-3000.Image source, SBUImage caption, The remnants of the wing from a glide bomb guidance kitBall and Proops both confirmed verified photos of munition fragments obtained by BBC Verify from Ukrainian authorities show part of a guidance kit that is compatible with the FAB-3000, which increases the weapon's accuracy and allows it to be fired from a greater distance from the target.International law experts told BBC Verify that Russia had committed a war crime if it knowingly attacked rescue workers.Ben Saul, professor of international law at the University of Sydney, said this "appears to be either a deliberate attack on civilians or civilian objects - a war crime - or an indiscriminate attack - also a war crime".Prof Samuel Moyn of Yale University said "directly targeting rescuers or their equipment is a gross violation of international humanitarian law". Precautions have to be taken to ensure that strikes target combatants rather than others, he added.Additional reporting by Margaryta Maliukova, BBC Monitoring

schema.headline: Komyshuvakha: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after strikes that killed 57

title: London City forward Izzy Goodwin receives first England call-up
description: London City Lionesses forward Izzy Goodwin has been named in the England squad for the first time for the World Cup qualifying play-off against Ukrain
body: London City Lionesses forward Izzy Goodwin has been named in the England squad for the first time for the World Cup qualifying play-off against Ukraine.The 23-year-old has been in great form this month and scored in front of England manager Sarina Wiegman at Emirates Stadium on Sunday in a 1-1 draw with Arsenal."We have always see her as a huge talent with potential," Wiegman told BBC Radio 5 Live. "I think London City are developing really well in the games they have showed. She is tall and can head a ball attacking-wise, but also defending. "She is really quick with her feet and can score goals. I really want to see her in our environment, what she can bring and how close she is to the level that we expect."There is also a first call-up for goalkeeper Katie Cox, on loan at Nottingham Forest from Chelsea, while Manchester United midfielder Ella Toone returns.Manchester City duo Niamh Charles and Alex Greenwood, who is injured, are among those to miss out.The Lionesses play Ukraine in Spain on 1 December before hosting them at Wembley on 5 December. The winner qualifies for next year's Women's World Cup."We know what's at stake in these games and our focus is on producing two strong performances to secure our place at the World Cup," said Wiegman."We have worked hard to put ourselves in this position and now we have to finish the job. "Ukraine will provide a challenge and we will prepare with the same focus and determination that we always do."Chelsea defender Lucy Bronze could make her 150th appearance at Wembley in the second leg.England travel to Pinatar, Spain a few days before the first leg and opted not to play a friendly match during this extended international break."The first part of the block we are [at St George's Park]. We have training sessions and a period of time where we can do some tactical stuff," added Wiegman. "We also selected more players so that helps us create situations where we can train things and everyone is important. I'm really excited to get ready for these games."Goalkeepers: Katie Cox (Nottingham Forest on loan from Chelsea), Hannah Hampton (Chelsea), Khiara Keating (Liverpool).Defenders: Lucy Bronze (Chelsea), Jess Carter (Gotham FC), Grace Fisk (Liverpool), Taylor Hinds (Arsenal), Maya Le Tissier (Manchester United), Esme Morgan (Washington Spirit), Poppy Pattinson (London City Lionesses), Leah Williamson (Arsenal). Midfielders: Laura Blindkilde Brown (Manchester City), Grace Clinton (Manchester City), Erica Meg Parkinson (North Carolina Courage), Lexi Potter (Chelsea), Georgia Stanway (Arsenal), Ella Toone (Manchester United), Keira Walsh (Chelsea).Forwards: Aggie Beever-Jones (Chelsea), Freya Godfrey (London City Lionesses), Izzy Goodwin (London City Lionesses), Lauren Hemp (Manchester City), Beth Mead (Manchester City), Jess Park (Manchester United), Alessia Russo (Arsenal).

schema.headline: London City forward Izzy Goodwin receives first England call-up

title: Tony Mowbray: Blackburn Rovers boss steps back over health issues
description: Blackburn Rovers head coach Tony Mowbray has stepped back from his role with the Championship club amid health issues.The 62-year-old returned for a s
body: Blackburn Rovers head coach Tony Mowbray has stepped back from his role with the Championship club amid health issues.The 62-year-old returned for a second spell in June having previously spent five years managing Rovers between 2017 and 2022.Mowbray had previously taken time out of the game during his time as Birmingham City boss in early 2024 following a health scare, and later revealed he had been undergoing treatment for bowel cancer.Rovers said Damien Johnson and Mike Dodds would take responsibility for first-team duties "for the time being"."Unfortunately, due to health issues, I have to step back from my role as head coach of Blackburn Rovers," Mowbray said in a statement., external"I'm immensely proud of this group of players. Their dedication and professionalism have given us some memorable performances and wins, and I've loved working with them."Thank you to my coaching staff for all your hard work and for the support you've given me. It's been a pleasure working alongside you."To the fans, thank you for the way you've supported me and the team this season. I've always tried to give you a team that you can be proud of. Your support has meant a great deal to me."Mowbray has transformed Blackburn this season, after a they hovered around the relegation places for much of last term before eventually finishing 20th in the Championship and five points above the drop zone.They are currently 13th in the Championship table having won six of their 15 league games and three points outside the play-offs.The announcement comes before Sunday's Lancashire derby against Burnley at Turf Moor, which was set to be Mowbray's 900th game in management as well as his 63rd birthday.

schema.headline: Tony Mowbray: Blackburn Rovers boss steps back over health issues

title: Trump says Alaska voters chose the wrong Dan Sullivan. What does data show?
description: ByJake Horton, Thomas Copeland and Wesley StephensonBBC VerifyAlmost two weeks after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterm elections, votes ar
body: ByJake Horton, Thomas Copeland and Wesley StephensonBBC VerifyAlmost two weeks after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterm elections, votes are still being counted in the race to elect a senator in Alaska, with Democratic candidate Mary Peltola ahead of her Republican rival - Senator Dan S Sullivan.This Senate contest has drawn scrutiny after another Dan Sullivan entered the race earlier this year - with ballot papers listing both the incumbent Dan S Sullivan and a Daniel J Sullivan Jr.Republicans have said this could have confused voters, prompting an unsuccessful legal challenge and President Donald Trump claiming votes for "the fake Dan Sullivan" were supposed to be for "the real Dan Sullivan".US media has not forecasted a winner in the race - the last Senate seat still without a winner after the 3 November election. But with 98% of the vote counted, even if Senator Dan S Sullivan's votes were combined with Daniel J Sullivan Jr's votes, this would still not overcome Peltola's lead. Alaska uses a ranked-choice voting system, which means voters can vote for five candidates in order of preference. If no candidate reaches more than 50% of the first preference votes, then voters' other choices will be used to decide who wins.BBC Verify has analysed voting data showing voters' second choices. It shows that over a third of voters who put Daniel J Sullivan Jr first left their second choice blank.The next highest second-choice preference was for the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola - receiving nearly twice as many second-choice votes as the Republican Dan S Sullivan.This calls into question claims that Republican voters may have been confused about which Sullivan they were voting for.Why midterm vote-counting is taking so long in America's largest stateHow did two Dan Sullivans end up in the race?Republican Dan S Sullivan has held the US Senate seat in Alaska since 2015 and was running for his third term.Daniel J Sullivan Jr - a retired school teacher from a remote fishing village in Alaska - entered the race in May and has run a low-key campaign.A New York Times story, external published the week before Election Day claimed that Democratic operatives with links to the Peltola campaign had tried to recruit "spoiler" candidates in the Senate race, including Daniel J Sullivan Jr.The report said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team also tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the reporting.Peltola has denied all knowledge of the alleged "scheme" and Sullivan Jr has denied any links with the Peltola campaign.President Trump has posted multiple times on Truth Social since the election, claiming that the race has been "rigged".But experts note it's not an illegal tactic, if it was employed. "There is nothing to prevent a campaign from recruiting someone else to run, even if for political reasons," said Joshua Douglas, an election law expert at the University of Kentucky.Alaska Senate candidate denies knowing about alleged plot to put two Dan Sullivans on ballotImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Senator Sullivan was joined by President Trump at a campaign rally ahead of the voteHow does voting work in Alaska?Voters in Alaska select their first choice candidate, followed by options to rank up to four other candidates in order of preference."There is no specific law preventing people with the same name running, but many states have laws or regulations about how names appear on the ballot. One of those regulations was used in Alaska" said Ruth Greenwood, director of the election law clinic at Harvard Law School.On Alaskans' ballots the two Sullivans were listed as:- Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.- Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) IncumbentThere was a second registered Republican candidate, Gerald Heikes - who was also allegedly recruited into the race according to The New York Times.Image source, Alaska Division of ElectionsImage caption, A sample ballot for the US Senate election in AlaskaAs of Tuesday, Peltola holds 49.98% of the vote. In the event that Peltola were not to clear 50%, officials eliminate the candidate in last place and reallocate those ballots to the voters' next choices. This process continues until two candidates remain, with one clearing the 50% hurdle.Daniel J Sullivan Jr is the listed candidate in last place with 1.65% of the vote.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Democrat Mary Peltola's said on Saturday she will "decisively be elected" as Alaska's next senatorWhat does ranked-choice voting data show so far?Senator Dan S Sullivan and his allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters.Trump said last week: "Anybody that voted for that second Dan Sullivan, the fake Dan Sullivan, was supposed to be a vote for the real Dan Sullivan".Of the ballots analysed by BBC Verify that ranked Daniel J Sullivan Jr first, 38% of them recorded no valid second choice.We do not know how many of these voters may have thought they had voted for the Senator Dan S Sullivan and then not ranked any other candidates.A further 29% of Daniel J Sullivan Jr voters ranked the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola second, almost double the 15% that ranked the incumbent Republican Senator Sullivan as second. "The likelihood that any confusion might play a significant role is diminished in Alaska," Richard Pildes, a professor of constitutional law at New York University, argues, "because any voter who was unsure which Dan Sullivan candidate they meant to vote for could rank them first and second."Additional reporting by Daniel Wainwright

schema.headline: Trump says Alaska voters chose the wrong Dan Sullivan. What does data show?

title: BBC launches educational show in Hausa for millions out of school in West Africa
description: BBC launches programme for children forced from school by bandits and poverty in West AfricaImage source, Ifiokabasi Ettang/BBCImage caption, Hadiza l
body: BBC launches programme for children forced from school by bandits and poverty in West AfricaImage source, Ifiokabasi Ettang/BBCImage caption, Hadiza left school at 13 to get married and now spends her time doing houseworkByMadina MaishanuBBC AfricaReporting fromGoronyoAs she pounds millet, 15-year-old Hadiza sings the English alphabet. It is a reminder of something that she desperately misses - going to school."Sometimes I write on the ground to practise and see if I'm still writing correctly," she says.One night, about two years ago, a group of armed men raided her village."They scared our cattle away and abducted a girl. We had to run away. We walked barefoot all the way here," she says.Since then she has lived in a displaced persons camp in Goronyo, a few kilometres from her home. For a short while she went to school here, but soon met a young man and, at the age of 13, stopped going to classes and got married."It's tradition here that once a girl is married, her education ends," she explains. Now she lives with her in-laws and helps look after the home. Although Nigerian law prohibits marriage under the age of 18, it is not always enforced.Image source, Ifiokabasi Ettang/BBCImage caption, Hadiza practises writing on the ground to make sure she doesn't forget the English alphabetHadiza is one of nearly 19 million children in Nigeria who are missing out on an education, according to estimates shared by Unesco in 2024. That's about one in four of the country's school-age children.Against this backdrop, the BBC World Service has launched Dars Hausa, an educational programme in the main language spoken in northern Nigeria, as well as neighbouring Niger, Cameroon and elsewhere in West Africa.It brings English, maths and science lessons to children across West Africa, via social media, local television partnerships and radio. Many people in the region get their news from the radio and nearly half of households in Nigeria have one, according to the charity Save the Children.Dars means "lesson" in Pashto and Dari, and it was first launched in those languages in 2023 for Afghan children barred from attending school. An Arabic version followed in February 2025.The reasons why so many Nigerian children are out of school are numerous and complex. Like Hadiza, 12-year-old Rukayya also lives in the displacement camp in Goronyo.Image source, Ifiokabasi Ettang/BBCImage caption, After Rukayya's father was killed, she gave up school to earn money instead "It pains me to see other children studying and going to school while I cannot," she says.As the eldest child, each day Rukayya goes out to gather firewood to sell and to beg so that her younger siblings can have something to eat."If my father was alive, I wouldn't have to go out and beg," she explains, saying some people mock her "but it doesn't stop me because it is our only way to survive."Bandits killed her father about a year ago in front of her, she says, and her family fled from their home to the camp.She and Hadiza are among 670,000 people in north-west and central Nigeria who have been forced from their homes by armed robbery and kidnappings, according to the International Organization for Migration.Three Girls: Lessons in Limbo features the stories of Hadiza and Rukayya - you can watch the full film on YouTube, externalSome attacks have been carried out by militant Islamist groups, but the majority in this region are by criminal gangs, known in Nigeria as bandits, who steal, kill and kidnap.The school that Hadiza once attended in Goronyo is the only one serving children in the camp and typically has about 50 students in each class.One of the teachers, Kamilu Sulaiman Jakada, says that even though lessons are free, only a tiny portion of the children attend, and even then sporadically, because parents tell him that "it is the children that are the breadwinners" and they need to earn money to eat.Image source, Ifiokabasi Ettang/BBCImage caption, Armed gangs, poverty and lack of funding all have a huge impact on children's education, says teacher Kamilu Sulaiman JakadaHe says the school does not have enough teachers or classrooms, explaining that funding is inconsistent and often comes from individuals or organisations rather than the government.The other challenge is the bandits. A gang once came to the school on motorbikes, shooting in the air, he says, and although no-one was hurt, many parents were scared and withdrew their children. That has been parents' reaction to attacks in some other parts of the country too.Every Nigerian child is meant to get nine years of free, compulsory education - six in primary and three in secondary school. Responsibility is shared between federal, state and local governments.But many schools are facing shortages and poorer families who cannot afford private education can struggle to pay for uniforms, books and transport.The crisis has built up over decades, with successive governments struggling to address chronic underfunding and poor oversight of resources.In addition, many children in the traditional Almajiri system, which provides Islamic education, are not taught subjects such as maths and science, and are considered by Unicef to be out of school.Image source, Ifiokabasi Ettang/BBCImage caption, Many of Nigeria's schools face shortages of teachers, classrooms and learning materials after years of underfunding and lack of oversightMinister of State for Education Prof Suwaiba Sa'id believes the number of children out of school is lower than has been reported, but admits that with Nigeria's growing population "the proper investment, the proper oversight, has not been done… I will not mention the names, but we know of two states that did not recruit a single teacher for eight years".She says that education is the government's "number-one priority" and initiatives such as Lumina are designed to help address "decades of neglect". Lumina aims to support one million girls by 2030, providing an accelerated learning programme for older girls who have missed years of formal education.She also says that "the government is doing everything possible" to deal with bandits and that "we have seen children that should be at school but are engaged in this banditry".In the meantime, it is children like Hadiza and Rukayya that the BBC World Service Dars Hausa programmes aim to help. Hadiza says she still has a dream to one day become a doctor "to help my fellow women".Dars Hausa will air on BBC News Hausa radio on Sundays at 06:45 West Africa Time, with a repeat at 20:45. The programme will also be available via BBC News Hausa's digital platforms, including YouTube, Facebook, X and Instagram.

schema.headline: BBC launches educational show in Hausa for millions out of school in West Africa

title: Has Gianni Infantino already won the Fifa presidential election?
description: Uefa has finally identified a candidate to take on Gianni Infantino in next year's Fifa presidential election.Less than 48 hours before Wednesday nigh
body: Uefa has finally identified a candidate to take on Gianni Infantino in next year's Fifa presidential election.Less than 48 hours before Wednesday night's deadline, European football's governing body announced that French Football Federation (FFF) president Philippe Diallo had received the unanimous support of its executive committee.A late surprise choice, Uefa claimed it had "full confidence in [him] to provide the leadership needed."But he is not the Frenchman some believe Uefa really wanted, as it seeks to remove Infantino in the wake of his failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.Senior figures in European football were known to have hoped to persuade Arsene Wenger - Fifa's head of global development - to stand against his own boss. Some felt that only he had the credibility and unifying potential to be able to pose a serious threat to Infantino's plans for a fourth term. But after the former Arsenal manager chose not to proceed, Uefa had no choice but to seek an alternative.So just how credible a challenger is Diallo? Does Infantino's position appear unassailable? And how could he still be stopped from winning another term?An administrator who has worked in French football since 1992 and became FFF president in 2023, Diallo is not a household name. But he has at least ensured that Infantino will not be unopposed, and has already shown he is not afraid to stand up to him.In September, Diallo claimed the Fifa president had "seriously damaged the image and unity of football", and said "trust has been broken" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) sell-off plot.Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister says Diallo is a "candidate who can instigate real, meaningful and lasting reform" within the governing body."We've always made it very clear that our objectives and motivations are driving culture change. That means wide-ranging, systemic reform of football governance rather than simply the replacement of an individual leader," McAllister told BBC Sport."I've known Philippe since we were both elected to Uefa's executive committee, and he's an intelligent, honest, sharp-minded football person with an impressive experience of governance in one of the world's football power-houses. Most importantly, he is a person of integrity... Philippe is a fantastic advocate for the change agenda that football needs, and I know his campaign will reflect that."Infantino remains the favourite to win a majority of the 211 votes, and is thought to have the support of most of Africa (54 members), Asia (47) and South America (10).However, there are hopes at Uefa that Diallo - whose father was a Senegalese boxing champion who represented France in the 1960 Olympics - could enjoy significant support in parts of Africa and beyond.But it is unclear precisely how many of Uefa's full 55-strong membership will back Diallo. Uefa only approached him about standing in the past week, and senior officials at some European national associations have also told BBC Sport they are frustrated with the failure to find a higher-profile candidate sooner.Speaking anonymously, one said they only learned about Diallo's potential candidacy on Sunday, and that while they were supportive of him, "it would have been helpful if we'd had someone much earlier" and "a lot of eggs were put in the Wenger basket." They also made the point that Diallo was yet to publish a manifesto, and questioned whether he could really win. Another expressed similar sentiments, saying Diallo was a good man, but "not seen as a heavyweight". They claimed that Uefa had "lost the momentum. The process hasn't been great. I really hope they've got a rabbit to pull out of the hat."Diallo claims he had the backing of countries beyond Europe. "It is now up to me and my team to go and convince those on other continents, but already...I have received spontaneous signs of strong support which will be revealed in the coming days", he said on Tuesday. McAllister is optimistic: "I have no doubt whatsoever that we will collectively mount a powerful campaign with the objective of winning the election next March". she said."The really critical period comes next, once candidate nominations close and eligibility checks are complete."Despite high-profile critics like Germany manager Jurgen Klopp - who this week said "the opinion is unanimous that a change would make sense" - Infantino does appear to be in a position of strength.As recently as August it all seemed very different when the heads of three confederations - Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America - signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception".Amid an increasingly acrimonious civil war, Infantino seemed vulnerable. But the revolt against him then suffered some setbacks.Uefa called off a threatened boycott of Fifa competitions, and then potential rivals such as Concacaf chief Victor Montagliani decided not to stand. Aleksander Ceferin chose to stand for a fourth term as Uefa president rather than challenge Infantino directly.Meanwhile, Infantino's position as the incumbent enabled him to embark on what has appeared to be a world tour, shoring up support. His chances of re-election received another major boost when he proposed to increase the amount of money handed out by Fifa for football development across the world by £2.6 billion.Sheikh Salman, the head of the Asian Football Confederation, then performed a U-turn, endorsing Infantino, who soon after told the BBC he had the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football. "I'm a professor of politics so I never assume that there's a runaway favourite to win any election", insists McAllister."There are plenty of twists and turns to come in this story between now and the election at Fifa's Congress next year."As I've said all along, this is about structural change and a commitment to modernising the way in which football is governed so it benefits all who play and watch. Whoever wins the presidential election next year, that imperative will remain and we will hold the new president accountable for much-needed change.""The current weaknesses of global football governance have been brutally exposed of late. This has helped coalesce and unite opposition to Gianni Infantino, but also to articulate the widely-held demands that things must change."So with just four months until the presidential election, where could Infantino still run into difficulties?Litigation is arguably the most obvious. As part of its wider plan to remove Infantino, Uefa has filed court documents in the US, which includes a potential criminal complaint against him in Switzerland for alleged financial mismanagement. So far, the legal action has not appeared to trouble him. But some senior figures in the European game remain hopeful it could still force Fifa to hand over evidence related to FFE that could prove damaging to Infantino's re-election prospects.There is pressure from elsewhere in football. Fifa has already agreed to make "key documents" relating to the FFE plan available to members of its council. Infantino's critics believe this disclosure may reveal details that could increase the pressure on him before the election. Last month, the Norwegian Football Federation also submitted a three-part ethics complaint to Fifa regarding the awarding of a Peace Prize to US President Donald Trump, the Folarin Balogun case at the World Cup, and the FFE plot. The Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections means scrutiny from beyond football too. Earlier this year, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee launched an inquiry into Infantino's ties with Trump. In September, a spokeswoman said Infantino and FIfa's co-operation with the investigation had been "woefully inadequate." But now, armed with extra powers, they could force him to hand over relevant documents or give evidence.Recent months have also seen a series of potentially damaging stories emerge in the media about various aspects of Infantino's leadership. So far they seem to have done little harm to his re-election chances, with Fifa claiming "it is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine [him]". But the scrutiny is likely to continue.Could Infantino even be ruled ineligible to stand? According to Portuguese lawyer Miguel Maduro - a former head of Fifa's governance committee - Infantino should not be allowed to be a candidate in the election as Fifa rules limit presidents to three terms. In 2022, Fifa's Council agreed that his first period in office - between 2016 and 2019 - should not count as he was effectively completing the remainder of Blatter's term after his resignation. But as Maduro has said, a national association or confederation would need to challenge this decision at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).Japan Football Association honorary president, Kozo Tashima, has announced his intention to stand, along with former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega. But with uncertainty over how much support either man will have, it seems Diallo is the challenger most likely to test the strength of Infantino's supporter base. There is a danger that the vote against Infantino is split.It has not gone unnoticed at Fifa that as recently as March, Diallo was quoted congratulating Infantino when the Fifa president visited Paris, external to highlight a mini-pitch programme and the need for more football infrastructure globally. A lot has changed since then, however. And now the Frenchman has been tasked with finding a way of unseating Infantino, and becoming just the 10th Fifa president in its history.

schema.headline: Has Gianni Infantino already won the Fifa presidential election?

title: New Zealand tricks and annual leave - the lengths fans are going to for GTA 6
description: Grand Theft Auto fans have waited 13 long years for the latest edition of the game to be released - and going to extreme lengths to be ready for its l
body: Grand Theft Auto fans have waited 13 long years for the latest edition of the game to be released - and going to extreme lengths to be ready for its launch.GTA 6 will be released at midnight on Wednesday - and Victoria Evans, from West Sussex, is not leaving anything to chance.She has her alarm set for 0500, and has a day off booked. She says she put the game's release on her leave request form which was approved, she told BBC News, despite the fact her boss "doesn't know what GTA 6 is". She's far from the only one. For the game's launch day, HR software company BrightHR, external looked at absence data from more than 1.2 million employees from 70,000 businesses across the UK.It found GTA was mentioned in 4.6% of time-off requests by employees. Throughout November and December, it said an estimated 83,000 days had been booked off for the game.And booking leave is only one of the ways fans are making sure for the big day. Others are buying a new console to play it on or even pretending they're halfway around the world to get early access.Aside from taking time off, some gamers have also been discussing a technical loophole which could give them valuable extra hours of play before it officially unlocks in their country.Because GTA 6 will release at midnight local time in all regions, New Zealand will become one of the first places where it is available, due to it reaching midnight earliest because of its position near the international date line.   This has led to some investigating ways to "trick" their consoles into thinking they're based in the island country when they are in fact thousands of miles away.According to Google Trends, searches for the "GTA 6 New Zealand trick" have surged by more than 5,000% in the UK over the past month.Games journalist Vic Hood said many gamers would be looking to play earlier to "get in on the action as soon as possible", as well as to prevent spoilers."As New Zealand is 13 hours ahead of the UK, that's 13 hours of gameplay that has time to spread across the internet and potentially spoil some key story beats and in-game surprises," she said."Took an extra day of paid time off when I found this out," one fan posted on Reddit on the trick.It also means gamers would be playing the game at the much nicer time of 11:00 GMT, rather than having to stay up all night.But another Xbox user shared caution on Reddit, noting that while the loophole had been exploited for many years for other game releases, GTA 6 "might be the game where Microsoft finally does something about this 'exploit'" - which could include  banning players.GTA 6's developers Rockstar and publishers Take Two Interactive have not commented on the loophole, and neither have Sony nor Microsoft.Louise Wooldridge from Ampere Analysis said both Microsoft and Sony had "rules governing regional accounts and purchases" for the Xbox and PlayStation, adding that Sony's were "slightly more restrictive".Players who choose to use the workaround could therefore risk breaching those terms and conditions and potentially face restrictions on their accounts or lose access to their digital games.Some gamers will have to wait even longer than their console-playing counterparts to get their hands on GTA 6, as the game will not be available on PC at launch, similar to previous GTA releases."Spare a thought for the PC users who will have to live vicariously through others' YouTube videos and Twitch streams," gamer Stephen Finn told the BBC.A PS5 now costs from £520, while the more powerful PS5 Pro is nearly £790.Despite the hefty price tag, for some the temptation to join the community in playing what many have called the biggest game launch of the year, if not decade, has been too great.Reddit posts and videos, such as one by US YouTuber isoish, external, show fans buying consoles specifically to play the game."So, the only game I'm going to have on here is GTA," the content creator said in the video. "The whole PS5 is for GTA 6."After more than a decade of waiting, it seems some fans are determined not to waste a single minute of GTA 6's release - no matter the cost or extra effort.

schema.headline: New Zealand tricks and annual leave - the lengths fans are going to for GTA 6

title: Met Police missed opportunities stop predatory detective who ran rape unit, BBC finds
description: Warning: Contains details of violence, coercion and sexual abuse - and strong languageThe Metropolitan Police repeatedly missed opportunities to stop
body: Warning: Contains details of violence, coercion and sexual abuse - and strong languageThe Metropolitan Police repeatedly missed opportunities to stop a predatory detective inspector from sexually exploiting women whose cases he investigated, including one who married him and later died in unexplained circumstances, BBC Panorama can reveal.Warren Arter used his position - running a unit investigating sexual assaults in south-east London - to target women it was his job to protect.Two women, speaking out for the first time, have told Panorama how Arter groomed them. One says he raped her.In the case of his wife, Rebekah, he filmed her being sexually abused and distributed the footage. She died in Barbados two years ago, while on holiday with him. On Sunday, the BBC revealed how he lied about what happened on the Caribbean island.There were multiple investigations into Arter while he was employed by the Met. Now the former detective who led one of them has told the BBC that senior bosses tried to interfere with his inquiries, despite him having found potential victims.While Arter was suspended as a result of that investigation, he remained on full pay for seven years - before being sacked in 2023 for drug offences.The following year, the Met - having learned of his wife's death in Barbados - arrested him on his return to the UK for sexual offences alleged by another woman.Arter took his own life days later in HMP Wandsworth. Despite the evidence against him, the Met has not reviewed all the cases he handled.The upskirting image that was sent in March 2024 to a woman we are calling Layla should have led to Arter's arrest.Bail conditions or custody would have prevented him from taking his wife, Rebekah, to Barbados.On 28 June, Arter rang Rebekah's relatives from the island to tell them she had died.Rebekah had been escaping an abusive relationship in 2006 when the Met put then-Det Sgt Warren Arter in charge of investigating her former partner.Arter pursued Rebekah, they began a relationship and he quickly moved in with her.Her now-adult son, Elliot, says Arter initially made his mum feel "safer" but that his behaviour soon changed."He'd say to her: 'Get in the kitchen, make my dinner you slag. Make me a tea you [expletive] bitch,'" Elliot recalls.Arter would openly watch pornography on his tablet while he was in the living room with her, Elliot says.He also collected urine from Elliot, claiming he was testing it at the police lab to help the boy's promising football career - but Elliot now suspects it was an effort to hide Arter's drug use.Watch Panorama: The Predator in the Police on BBC One at 21:00 on Tuesday 17 November (not in Wales or Northern Ireland) or on iPlayerThe inquest into Rebekah's death heard evidence that use of sedatives had become so routine in the home she shared with Arter, that a daily smart-speaker reminder announced "G o'clock" - a reference to the date-rape drug GHB.In the years before she died, Arter had filmed and distributed videos of his wife being sexually abused. The BBC has seen some of them.Many show her unconscious or otherwise incapacitated while Arter insults her."You should get raped," he says, in one video.In another, Arter can be heard speaking to a man behind the camera, asking him to be quiet and saying "they go mad otherwise" - suggesting the video was being made for a wider audience.His crimes were so brazen that he sent abuse videos of Rebekah unsolicited to at least four women he knew.Two were women whose cases he had investigated - one of them was Layla.She had met Arter in 2010 after she reported being raped. His exploitation of her continued for more than a decade, up until she reported the upskirting image - which she had deleted - to staff from the IOPC.Both Layla, and her adult daughter who was with her when she spoke to the IOPC, say she identified the woman in the photo as Rebekah - whom she recognised from previous videos.The IOPC says the staff member has no record or recollection of being told the identity of the woman in the photo - and it did not have the authority to investigate as Arter was no longer a police officer.It did, however, tell the Metropolitan Police about the upskirting allegation.It is not clear when his bosses found out about the relationship, but some of his colleagues appear to have known early on.The BBC understands that four officers told the IOPC investigation they believed Arter had met Rebekah on a case. One said they knew Rebekah had been a victim of domestic abuse, but they refused to sign a statement.The Met told Panorama that the IOPC's subsequent report had found that Arter's colleagues knew of his relationship with Rebekah, but did not know he had met her in the course of his duties, therefore he was not subject to any misconduct proceedings.None of the various investigations into Arter led to criminal charges before he was arrested in 2024. On one occasion, he even received a payout after being arrested for harassment.The IOPC has now told the BBC that of 21 possible Arter victims it had identified by 2020, it assessed he had inappropriate contact or relationships with eight of them, including Layla and Rebekah.Panorama has, however, learned of at least one more alleged victim who says she was groomed and sexually exploited over 12 years.When Det Insp Jaysen Veeren tried to investigate Arter a decade ago, he says senior Met bosses tried to interfere with his work.Veeren was a fast-rising officer in the Met's Directorate of Professional Standards (DPS) - which investigates police misconduct - and says he was warned he would be a "fool" to join the team because of its reputation within the force."The DPS is referred to as 'the rats' - you eat your own," he says.But when, in 2016, he intercepted a Crimestoppers tip complaining about Arter's conduct with victims, he recalls telling his boss: "This is the case that I joined for."Initially, his investigation was well resourced and he travelled to Australia to interview a woman who said Arter had sex with her after she reported being sexually assaulted as a tourist in London.Veeren then cold-called other cases."We had one victim and, all of a sudden, you've got a second, third," he recalls. "It was quite obvious you're dealing with a predator."Arter had been able to visit many of the women alone. One woman told Veeren: "He may as well have walked into my house with his [penis] out".Veeren eventually arrested Arter and suspended him in December 2016 but Arter's phone had been wiped.He then designed a plan to contact all the women whose cases Arter had investigated, but says he was prevented from doing so and his team encountered "interference" from senior officers outside of the DPS.Emails seen by the BBC reveal his investigation was likened to a "witch hunt" by a detective chief inspector, who questioned its justification with the Met "haemorrhaging talent". A chief superintendent told Veeren's boss that staff felt the case was a "fishing expedition".The two senior officers - who have since left the force - told the BBC this was not interference and said they were acting on concerns of colleagues about how the investigation was being carried out.Veeren says he felt unable to widen his investigation and examine all of Arter's cases.He referred his case into Arter to the IOPC in the expectation it would do so, and later reported his concerns to the watchdog as part of a wider whistleblowing complaint - alleging corruption within the DPS.He resigned from the force in 2019 when he discovered none of his allegations would be upheld. The Met says his complaints to the IOPC had either been disproven or not corroborated.Within hours of their first meeting, Arter asked Layla to put her head in his lap and then he stroked her hair, while a PC drove them to a sexual assault referral centre.There, Arter was found by staff alone in the toilets with her.A doctor was so alarmed by his behaviour that she reported concerns to the Met about his intimacy with Layla.Layla has told us that Arter remained present while she had an internal medical examination.The Met failed to investigate or monitor the detective's ongoing contact with Layla, who at the time was a vulnerable alcoholic.Arter visited Layla dozens of times over the next few months, she tells us, sexually exploiting her during what he described as "therapy time".Panorama has learned that Arter told colleagues that Layla was becoming too attached to him.He was commended for victim care in her case - just as he had been in the domestic abuse case of his future wife, Rebekah.Even after Arter informed Layla that the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) had declined to authorise charges in July 2010, he continued to contact her - helping her with a successful compensation claim under a government-funded scheme.After Veeren referred his investigation to the IOPC, the watchdog described Layla as having been "groomed" by Arter.Layla says Arter, who by this time had been suspended, was telling her what to tell investigators. She did not provide them with a statement.Despite Layla's known vulnerability, and the evidence against Arter, it took three years for a file of evidence about his sexual misconduct to be sent to the CPS, which then declined to pursue criminal charges in 2020.It was a further three years before Arter appeared at a misconduct hearing - and only then for drug offences.He was finally dismissed from the Met in 2023 - have received at least £300,000 in pay while suspended. He kept his pension.However, despite having left the force, a decision to review Arter's alleged sexual misconduct was then made.In March 2024, IOPC staff visited Layla at home. She revealed Arter had sent her the upskirting image. By this point, she says she had begun to "wake up" to Arter's exploitation of her.The watchdog told the Met about the illegal image - but the force failed to arrest him.The Met told Panorama this was because of human error when using a new crime recording system.They say they found a variety of drugs and hidden CCTV cameras that Arter had rigged up.They also discovered photographs of Rebekah naked and bruised, involved in sexual acts, seemingly taken without her consent.On 2 July, Elliot and Lacey drove to Bexleyheath Police Station - the same station where Arter had worked.Staff were initially uninterested in Rebekah's death thousands of miles away, say the couple - and it was only when they mentioned Arter's name that officers became interested. "It was like chaos," Lacey says.The family say they were told the Met was considering sending officers out to Barbados to help the investigation.However, the BBC has been told that a senior Met boss from its Gold Command group was briefed that evening about the incident, in light of Arter's alleged offending, and a decision was taken not to send officers to the Caribbean island.The Met told the BBC it took this decision because no allegation of criminality had been made.Later that week, the Met visited Layla and interviewed her about Arter, where she disclosed he had raped her on one occasion and sexually assaulted her on another.Arter flew back to London from Barbados on 9 July and was arrested at Heathrow Airport, accused of rape, voyeurism and coercive control. He took his own life in prison three days later.Neither the Met nor the IOPC has ever released their investigation reports into Arter's sexual misconduct - despite Freedom of Information requests by the BBC.Arter was seen as the star detective in a unit lauded for its results investigating rape and sexual assault.But the Met has never investigated that unit's "sanction detection rates" - the proportion of reported crimes for which action was taken against suspects.In 2009, Conservative politician James Cleverly, then a Member of the London Assembly, said the unit had achieved rates of 96%.This is despite the figure being three times the London average and at a time when some officers were known to be systemically manipulating the recording of offences. The Met says it does not recognise the 96% figure.If you are in the UK and you have been affected by any of the issues in this story such as sexual abuse and violence, information and support is available at BBC Action LineDame Vera says there seems to be many missed opportunities to stop Arter, spanning from 2006 to 2024: "There must have been other people who knew exactly what was going on."Rebekah's family say the Met should investigate whether other men helped Arter abuse her.When she died the Met seized electronic devices from the house she had shared with Arter. Elliot says some of those devices have not been analysed in two years.His solicitor says a public inquiry is needed to reveal the full extent of Arter's offending."It's a disgrace for the Metropolitan Police, and it's also a dirty secret - one they want to keep hidden," says Sophie Naftalin.The Met told Panorama that Arter could have been arrested sooner and it was "deeply sorry" for the harm caused to victims by his repeated exploitation of his position for sexual purposes.It acknowledged progress with Arter's devices had been slow but said it was now being prioritised, and it encouraged anyone else who believes they were targeted to come forward.It added that the recording of rape cases was examined nationally in 2014 - and there have been significant changes to the scrutiny of crime figures.The IOPC says it regretted that its investigation took three years but it was a complex case involving delays out of its control. It added that the allegations were treated "extremely seriously" and resulted in referrals to the CPS.The CPS says it thoroughly reviewed this evidence but concluded there was no realistic prospect of conviction at that time.It says it did charge Arter with misconduct in public office before his death in 2024.In September 2025, the UK coroner in Rebekah's case issued what is known as a prevention of future deaths report.It said there was a risk that further deaths could occur unless action was taken.In response, the Met said it had already taken action to improve vetting and to tackle police officers abusing their powers.The IOPC said information had not been made available to it at the time of a specific risk to Rebekah, and that it had since strengthened its safeguarding procedures.Elliot says he has spent the past two years trying to get answers."I don't think I've grieved yet", he says."I don't know what will happen when that day will come."If you have more information about this story, you can reach Noel directly and securely through encrypted messaging app Signal on: +44 7809 334720, or by email at noel.titheradge@bbc.co.uk

schema.headline: Met Police missed opportunities stop predatory detective who ran rape unit, BBC finds

title: 'We're a capitalist society': Grindr defends $120 a month premium tier
description: The world's largest LGBTQ+ dating app, Grindr, has defended its $120 (£91) per month premium subscription service, which launches globally today.Edge
body: The world's largest LGBTQ+ dating app, Grindr, has defended its $120 (£91) per month premium subscription service, which launches globally today.Edge offers AI-powered services such as daily personalised profile recommendations that aim to provide better matches and limit scrolling.The company's CEO, George Arison, told BBC News it would be a "very different Grindr experience" which was aimed at a "small community of users" - and was unapologetic about its cost."I think we're a capitalist society, and everything hinges on whether you can afford it or not," he said.Grindr has long had a free service, and offers two additional tiers that cost between $22.99 and $44.99 per month.There was a mixed reaction from users BBC News spoke to in San Francisco to the  new, much more expensive version of the app."The current premium Grindr tier is already really expensive," said a user named Rybin, who told the BBC the company's newest offering "just seems really out of touch with the community.""I think that that's really disheartening, and it kind of leaves a bad taste in my mouth," said another user, Adrian. Both declined to give their last name."The cost doesn't bother me," said a user named Michael. "All of these apps have premium tiers so saying that Grindr shouldn't have that when like it exists across all these other apps used for connection doesn't make sense."He noted that high-end dating apps like The League can charge much more.Grindr has been experimenting with Edge for much of the last year in markets including the US, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand.On its earnings call earlier this month, the company said almost 400,000 users had registered for the service in the first 72 hours that it was available for testing.Inside Grindr, Edge is viewed as a way to drive future growth in an industry has struggled in recent years.For those who can afford it, the service promises to offer insights about a user's compatibility with prospective matches. It also resurfaces a user's past connections alongside summaries of previous interactions.The current $120 monthly fee comes after the company tested charging hundreds of dollars more than that. And Arison has left open the possibility of increasing the cost in the future.Arison told the BBC he's not concerned that intoducing an ultra-premium offering will pit "haves" against "have-nots" on the social networking platform.Edge users "being willing to pay more for that set of features will result in us being able to subsidise the product for everybody else," Arison said. "It's a choice that people make on whether they want to be on it." The use of AI to develop the Edge service is part of Grindr's attempt to become what it calls an "AI-first company."Arison said the company was investing in AI to ensure it can build products more quickly and  cheaply.In September, as the debate over AI safety raged throughout Silicon Valley, Arison told the BBC that his concerns about what he called an "anti-civilisational worldview at Anthropic" had prompted him to instruct some of his engineers to stop using Anthropic's technology.Anthropic is due to start selling shares to the public for the first time this week.Although Anthropic's Claude Code tools remain in use at Grindr now, Arison said the company is on track to completely phase it out of his company's workflows by next year.He said Grindr was once a very heavy user of Claude Code but that it was no longer the primary tool the use to write code."Anthropic's built an amazing amazing set of products, and they should be very proud of what they've done," Arison said. "They should aim to win with the awesome products they have, rather than regulatory capture that they're trying to win with, oftentimes."

schema.headline: 'We're a capitalist society': Grindr defends $120 a month premium tier
